analysis.investment_thesis: Accretion Pharma fails the Magic Formula's "good business" test decisively — a 0.65% ROE implies near-zero return on capital, which no amount of optical cheapness (P/E 8.11) can compensate for. The Magic Formula demands BOTH cheap AND good; this is neither demonstrably cheap on EBIT/EV nor remotely good on returns.
key_strengths: Low headline P/E of 8.11 suggests potential earnings yield if sustainable
Operating in defensive pharma sector with structural India tailwinds
key_risks: ROE of 0.65% implies ROIC almost certainly below 5% — fails Magic Formula quality bar
Micro-cap (₹73.6 Cr) with zero institutional ownership (FII/DII = 0%) signals no smart-money validation
P/E may be masking one-time items or trailing earnings that are not repeatable
red_flags: No EBIT or enterprise value disclosed to verify earnings yield
Zero institutional coverage in a capital-hungry pharma business
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The Magic Formula ranks companies on earnings yield (EBIT/EV) AND return on capital. Accretion fails the second filter catastrophically: 0.65% ROE means the business is destroying value relative to its cost of capital. Even if leverage is low and ROIC runs modestly above ROE, we are still nowhere near the >20% ROIC threshold I require. A cheap price on a bad business is a value trap — "you get what you pay for, slowly."

On the first filter, P/E 8.11 looks superficially attractive but without EBIT and enterprise-value data I cannot confirm an earnings yield above my 12% hurdle, and a ₹73.6 Cr micro-cap pharma with sub-1% ROE is the archetype of a name that screens cheap for a reason. Pass — the Magic Formula universe has hundreds of names with far better combined rankings.
